text:
We are “misplacing our trust” in the Cop climate summits and their “capacity to deliver consequential change”, according to Robert Macfarlane in this year’s Reith lectures.
In comments recorded before this week’s failure of the 31st UN climate summit to deliver an agreement on action to combat global heating, the bestselling author said he saw “much more hope” in emerging alliances such as the Santa Marta process, which is a smaller group of countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels as soon as possible.
“I would urge us to support these forms of collective reimagining away from ossified institutions that have failed to deliver,” said Macfarlane during the debate that followed his first Reith lecture, which will be broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 24 November. Diplomats, scientists and activists including Al Gore have called for reform of the Cop’s requirement for a consensus after the failure of this year’s talks.
Inhis lecture, Macfarlane, a professor of literature and environmental humanities at the University of Cambridge whose books, including Underland and Is a River Alive?, explore global environmental crises, argues we must challenge the pervasive but wrong “human superiority complex” in western thinking which has supported centuries of planetary abuse, leading to the entwined climate and extinction crises.
The planetary crisis we are facing is a “crisis of the imagination as well as legislation”, said Macfarlane, because of a “default planetary operating system” that has arisen from Aristotle onwards and promotes the idea that humans are separate from the rest of nature, superior to it, and can thrive by conquering it.
The idea of human superiority spread by Christianity, the philosophers of the Enlightenment and Europeans who colonised other continents is so ubiquitous that it is barely seen by citizens or governments, and is embedded in everyday language, from “livestock” to “natural resources”.
“Governments speak easily of datacentres as critical national infrastructure but don’t seem to recognise that river systems and pollinator populations are also critical national infrastructure,” said Macfarlane.
He told the audience after the first of his four 2026 Reith lectures that the “end-times tech bro” was today’s “most charismatic and frightening contemporary expression” of the human superiority complex, and he criticised “planet B thinking” for promoting the idea of establishing a human colony on Mars.
“It is the ultimate act of consumption and disposal. ‘Hey bro, this planet’s done. Chuck it in the trash, let’s go and find another.’ Mars colonisation is the oligarch’s rapture dream,” he said.
Macfarlane is using his four lectures to reveal a burgeoning alternative way of thinking about our place on the planet which conceives of humans as not standing atop a hierarchical ladder but as nodes on a web of life that is connected to everything. Many Indigenous societies have practised such thinking for millennia but in the west it was first expressed, said Macfarlane, by the German polymath Alexander von Humboldt when he was exploring the Andes in 1802 and realised that “nature is a living whole” of which people were one small part.
Despair at seemingly unstoppable global heating, oil wars and a chaotic technological arms race was “a luxury”, said Macfarlane, but he warned “hope” – “a verb with its sleeves rolled up” – involved real hard work.
“The first thing that anybody who is feeling helpless and hopeless should do is join a collective – find the folk who also love trees, who care about birds, who recognise that our life is absolutely inextricably tied to part of that larger living world,” he said. “Join your river guardianship group, drag the tyres out of the river on a Saturday morning. The best antidote to despair is repair. Start small; we build big.”
Macfarlane said young people, many of whom may succumb to the opposite of hope, which was not despair but “numbness”, must not be “terrified” by abstract threats but given opportunities to access nature and do hands-on work. He suggested partnering every British school with a farm and a tree-planting project “so that children are planting the trees that they then see grow throughout their lives”.
Asked about non-violent direct action by an audience member who had served a prison sentence for her role in Just Stop Oil protests that temporarily closed the M25 motorway, he said he would be willing to go to prison if he believed his peaceful direct action could have more impact than his writing, teaching and campaigning outside prison.
“What needs to change is not the nature of the protests that you and others have undertaken, which is peaceful protest, it’s the legislative environment that has sprung up around peaceful protest, particularly in the last three to five years,” he said, condemning the arrest and imprisonment of people in Britain for peaceful environmental protest.

רוברט מקפרלן, פרופסור לספרות ומדעי הרוח הסביבתיים באוניברסיטת קיימברידג', הצהיר בסדרת הרצאות כי האמון בוועידות האקלים השנתיות של ה-Cop כיעילות ומשנות מציאות הוא שגוי. לדבריו, יש לתלות תקווה בבריתות אלטרנטיביות קטנות יותר, כמו תהליך סנטה מרטה, שבהן חברות מדינות המחויבות להוצאת דלקים מאובנים משימוש בהקדם האפשרי. מקפרלן טען כי המשבר הסביבתי נובע בין היתר מ"תסביך עליונות אנושי" שורשי בתרבות המערבית, הרואה באדם כיצור הנפרד מהטבע והשולט בו.

בהתייחסו למצב, ציין מקפרלן כי ייאוש הוא מותרות, וכי הדרך להתמודד איתו היא הצטרפות לקבוצות פעילות מקומיות וקהילתיות הדואגות לסביבה. הוא הוסיף כי יש לחבר צעירים לטבע באמצעות עבודה מעשית וחקלאות, במקום לזרוע בהם פחד מול איומים מופשטים. בנוסף, התייחס למחאות סביבתיות בבריטניה וקרא לרפורמה בסביבה החקיקתית הפוגעת בחופש המחאה השקטה והשלומית.
